question: What happens to bond market price when interest rates rise?
before: Fundamental inverse relationship. Existing bonds with lower fixed coupons become less attractive, prices fall to adjust effective yield upward. D confuses credit risk with interest rate risk.
after:
Concept: Bond prices move inversely to interest rates. When market interest rates rise, existing bonds with fixed coupon payments become less attractive relative to newly issued bonds offering higher yields, so their prices must fall to compete.

Step-by-step: Consider a bond paying a fixed 5% coupon. If new bonds are issued at 7%, investors will only buy the old 5% bond if its price drops. That price reduction increases the effective yield (yield-to-maturity) of the old bond, making it competitive again with the new 7% bonds.

Why this is correct: Option B correctly identifies the inverse relationship between interest rates and bond prices. This is a foundational principle in fixed income markets—when rates rise, bond prices fall, and vice versa.

Why the others are wrong: A (Price rises) reverses the relationship entirely and shows a misunderstanding of bond valuation. C (Price stays same) ignores the mechanism by which bond markets clear when rates change. D (Depends on credit rating) conflates interest rate risk with credit risk; credit rating affects the spread or premium demanded, but the inverse interest-rate relationship holds for all bonds regardless of rating.

Intuition: Bond prices and interest rates are seesaw mechanics—equity analysts must understand this because rising rate regimes typically pressure fixed-income portfolios, affect discount rates in DCF models, and signal shifts in monetary policy that ripple through equity valuations and cost of capital across the market.
